key_insight: A differentiable DDAM formulation enables topology optimization to use Navy shock-certification criteria directly as design constraints.
engineering_relevance: Designing for shock response inside the optimization loop can reduce shipboard component material while avoiding layouts that perform well in compliance but fail certification criteria.
method: Differentiate DDAM spectral displacement through natural frequency and modal participation.
Use Fox–Kapoor eigenvalue sensitivities, Nelson eigenvector sensitivities, and automatic differentiation.
Constrain the mean of the two lowest eigenvalues to stabilize response near the frequency floor.
evidence_signal: Three equipment-frame certification problems removed 43.2–46.1% of design-domain material while keeping the certifying NRL Sum within 0.41% of the Navy allowable.
watch_item: Repeated low-frequency modes can cause acceptance-boundary oscillations; the added eigenvalue constraint stabilized the response but still ended up to 0.5% above the allowable.
paper_title: Topology optimization of shipboard components for Navy shock certification via the Dynamic Design Analysis Method
